To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

codes of conduct are not a sufficient tool to improve labour standards, because they are not applied to non-factory production, and because they are not designed to regulate the labour process of the majority of workers in the industry.
the globalisation of the garment industry is taking place in a context where labour is increasingly flexibilised and informalised.

codes of conduct are ineffective in the Indian garment industry due to a mismatch between the ‘codes of conduct’ and the ‘codes of practice’, which is a result of a complex interplay of local architectures of production and the firm’s strategies to minimize its responsibility towards workers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the ‘governance’ of labour, and the ways in which labour standards are actually governed in the global garment industry.
the question of how labour standards are actually produced, and how this is mediated by the firm.
the ‘globalisation’ and ‘localisation’ of labour standards in India.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
codes of conduct are not the answer to improving labour standards in the Indian garment industry.

, while codes of conduct have been largely unsuccessful in improving labour conditions in the Indian garment industry, they have been highly successful at imposing a new form of labour control on workers.
the ‘codes of conduct’ approach is ineffective in improving labour standards.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
codes of conduct are only effective when they are designed as codes of practice, i.e., when they can be effectively imposed on labour.
the firm is a fundamental prism through the which to study labour.
the ‘globalisation’ process is characterised by a growing informalisation of production and labour standards.
The main takeaway from our work is that
codes of conduct are not the only, nor even the most important, means to regulate labour.
the ‘global’ garment industry is in reality a ‘multilocal’ industry, and this has important implications for the way we understand and study labour and labour rights.
codes of conduct have limited impact on labour standards because they are not designed to address the main challenges faced by workers in the global garment industry.
